questions.enonce_markdown:
State FOUR differences between a current account and a deposit account.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Both are accounts opened with a commercial bank, but they serve different purposes: a current account is for daily payments, a deposit account is for saving.

| | Current account | Deposit account |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | For frequent receipts and payments of a business or an individual. | For saving money that is not needed immediately. |
| Cheque book | A cheque book is issued, and payments are made by cheque. | Usually no cheque book; money is withdrawn with a withdrawal slip or passbook (or a card). |
| Interest | Usually **no interest** is paid on the balance. | **Interest** is paid on the balance. |
| Withdrawals | Money can be withdrawn at any time, without notice, and as often as wished. | Withdrawals may be limited or may require notice, so it is less easy to get the money. |
| Overdraft | An **overdraft** may be allowed by agreement with the bank. | No overdraft facility. |
| Bank charges | The bank charges for keeping the account (commission on transactions). | Charges are few or none. |

(Any four rows are sufficient for full marks.)

**Conclusion.** The current account gives ease of payment; the deposit account gives a return (interest) on savings.

questions.enonce_markdown:
With the use of any TWO examples, differentiate between general crossing and special crossing on cheques.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A **crossed cheque** has two parallel transverse lines drawn across its face. The crossing is an order to the paying bank that the cheque must be paid **into a bank account** and not over the counter in cash. This protects the drawer if the cheque is lost or stolen. There are two main types of crossing.

**1. General crossing.** Two parallel lines are drawn across the cheque, with or without the words "and Company" or "Not negotiable". No bank is named, so the cheque can be paid into the account of the payee at **any bank**.

*Example:* Mr Ngu draws a cheque for 150,000 Frs in favour of Mrs Tabi and draws two parallel lines across it, with the words "& Co". Mrs Tabi can pay it into her account in any bank.

**2. Special crossing.** The name of a **particular bank** is written between the two parallel lines (the lines themselves are not necessary). The paying bank must pay the cheque only to the bank named in the crossing, for the account of the payee.

*Example:* Mr Ngu writes "Bank A, Douala" between the two parallel lines on a cheque of 150,000 Frs. The cheque can be paid only through Bank A, Douala, and Mrs Tabi must have an account there or ask her own bank to collect it from Bank A.

| | General crossing | Special crossing |
|---|---|---|
| Bank named? | No. | Yes, a named bank is written in the crossing. |
| Payment | Into the account at any bank. | Only through the bank named. |
| Safety | Safe, but less safe than the special crossing. | Safer, because the cheque goes to one named bank only. |

**Conclusion.** A crossing makes a cheque safer than an open cheque, and a special crossing is the safer of the two.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Briefly explain any TWO of the following in insurance:

i) Burglary,

ii) Consequential loss,

iii) Fidelity guarantee and

iv) Jettison.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Each of these is either a type of insurance cover or a risk dealt with in insurance. (Any two are required; all four are given.)

**i) Burglary.** Burglary insurance covers the insured against **loss of property stolen when thieves break into the premises by force** (for example from a shop or an office). The insurer pays the value of the goods stolen and repairs the damage to doors and windows.

**ii) Consequential loss.** Also called **loss of profits insurance**. It pays the business for the **loss of income and the continuing expenses (rent, wages) that follow a major disaster** such as a fire, when production or sales stop until the firm is back in operation. It is taken in addition to a fire policy.

**iii) Fidelity guarantee.** An insurance by which the employer is repaid for **money or goods lost through the dishonesty (theft, fraud) of an employee**, for example a cashier or a storekeeper, who is in a position of trust.

**iv) Jettison.** The **throwing of part of the cargo (or equipment) overboard from a ship in danger** in order to lighten it and save the ship and the rest of the cargo. In marine insurance such a loss is shared by all the owners of the cargo and the ship, under the rule of general average.

**Conclusion.** These covers reduce the financial effect of theft, disaster, dishonesty and sea risks on a business.
